docs.title: hiprofile
docs.text:
hiprofile fits global HI line profiles with the six-parameter model of Stewart, Blyth & de Blok (2014, A&A 567, A61) and Bayesian model comparison. A single call fits a whole list of spectra in parallel:

hiprofile fit spectra.txt --config survey.yaml --jobs 32 --out results/

and writes, per spectrum, an HDF5 file with weighted posterior samples (including W50, W20, flux and systemic velocity), evidences for N = 0, 1, 2, ... components and Chebyshev baseline orders K, the detection probability, quality metrics and flags, and optionally plots. Over all spectra it builds a catalogue (FITS/Parquet/CSV) and an HTML report.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
uv pip install "hiprofile[all]"      # JAX, dynesty, UltraNest, matplotlib, pyarrow
uv pip install hiprofile             # minimal: compiled kernel, SMC and nautilus

Extras: [jax], [gpu] (CUDA JAX), [samplers], [plots], [parquet], [dev].

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: command purpose hiprofile fit fit a spectrum list (list file, glob, catalogue with paths or cube positions) hiprofile simulate generate test spectra with known truth hiprofile validate run the validation stages (SBC, detection, misspecification, injection) hiprofile report build catalogue and HTML report from existing results hiprofile plot plots for single or flagged spectra from stored samples

docs.title: ALFALFA α.40 refitted
docs.text:
All 15 041 sources with HIcode 1 or 2 of the ALFALFA α.40 catalogue (Haynes et al. 2011) were refitted with hiprofile and compared with the catalogue, source by source. The result is data/alfalfa_a40.csv (one row per source, columns below) with data/alfalfa_a40_summary.json.

python benchmarks/alfalfa_survey.py fit --out DIR --n 0 --jobs 4
python benchmarks/alfalfa_survey.py compare --out DIR --catalog data/alfalfa_a40.csv --figures docs/img

fit downloads the spectra from NED (Hanning smoothed, baseline subtracted, 5.2 km/s channels), cuts ±1000 km/s around the catalogue velocity, and fits them with model.response: boxcar+hanning, N ≤ 2 and otherwise the default configuration. Fits at 0ba7787 (median 10.6 s per spectrum on one core, about 44 h of CPU in total), spectrum conversion at d114eb0; the 120 spectra of the follow-up below were refitted at d053ea5 with the current defaults (symmetric outlier background, negative runs masked, components contained in the window). Downloads and fits resume where they stopped.

Data preparation. Three properties of the NED files matter:

  • Blanked channels carry a flux of exactly 0 (14 % of the spectra have some in the window, median 22 channels); they are masked.
  • ***** marks a value that overflows its column. In the baseline column it is harmless, in the flux column (over 10 Jy) the channel is masked.
  • Galactic HI and the high-velocity clouds reach a few hundred km/s and are Jy-bright; the window starts at 350 km/s. 2 sources leave fewer than 64 usable channels and are skipped, 3 have no spectrum in NED.

docs.text:
15 036 spectra fitted, none failed; 14 824 detected (P(detect) > 0.5).

Median and robust scatter over the detected sources; "naive" and "Springob" are the classical widths that hiprofile measures on the same spectra around the fitted component (see validation).

  • Fluxes and velocities agree with the catalogue to better than 1 % and 1 km/s in the median at every S/N.
  • Widths agree to about 1 % from S/N 12. Below, the posterior median is 3–5 % wider than the catalogue, where the naive measurement on the same spectra is not: the shrinkage of faint lines toward the typical width of the prior (see the conditional-bias study in the validation).
  • Detection: 99.5 % of the HIcode 1 and 95.0 % of the HIcode 2 sources. The undetected bright sources lie below cz = 350 km/s, behind the Galactic cut.
  • The W50 pull (difference over the combined errors) is narrower than a unit normal (robust width ≈ 0.55): both measurements see the same noise, so their difference is smaller than independent errors would make it.
  • N = 2 is preferred for 7 % of the HIcode 1 sources, rising to most sources above S/N 300: bright profiles show more structure than the model, or a neighbour is in the window.
  • Flags: 20.5 % of the detections; ppp 7.4 %, prior_dominated 6.1 %, prior_edge 5.5 %, wiggle 3.5 %, multimodal 2.7 %, residual_structure 1.6 %, rfi 0.6 %.

docs.title: Disagreements
docs.text:
15 % of the detections differ from the catalogue W50 by more than 30 % (10 % of HIcode 1 and 34 % of HIcode 2 above cz = 1000 km/s), 7.4 % in cz by more than 40 km/s. 39 % of them are flagged, against 17 % of the rest.

The largest differences fall into a few groups:

  • A bright neighbour. The catalogue source is a faint, narrow line next to a much brighter galaxy in the same spectrum; with N = 1 the fit describes the bright one (e.g. AGC 227952, 732898). These need the maps the ALFALFA team used; a single spectrum cannot tell which line belongs to the position.
  • Strong narrow spikes that the RFI pre-stage leaves unmasked and the fit takes for the line (AGC 233790, 721520, 181695); mostly flagged unresolved, ppp or prior_edge.
  • Faint HIcode 2 lines where narrow and wide solutions compete (prior_dominated, multimodal), and strongly lopsided profiles where the catalogue measures each horn at half its own height.
  • Nearby sources (cz < 1000 km/s, 299 detections): N = 2 in 16 % and W50 differences above 30 % in 19 %, from the wing of Galactic HI and from extended, bright galaxies.

docs.title: A positive profile on a negative baseline
docs.text:
Every component is positive by construction (S ≥ 0, f in [0, 1], |α| ≤ 1, positive kernels), but in 0.4 % of the detections a profile sat on a baseline more than 5 rms below zero, so that the sum dipped below −3 rms: the fit reproduced a dip next to strong continuum, or an RFI feature, as "profile minus baseline". In 0.6 % a component reached the edge of the window. The RFI pre-stage found these dips (outlier probability ≈ 1) but kept them, because runs longer than rfi.max_width (20 km/s) are protected as possible lines. Two changes followed: the protection is now limited to runs above the pre-stage model, with a symmetric outlier background, and every profile component must lie entirely inside the window (priors.contain, see Priors). On the 120 affected spectra (detected fractions; the last row counts detections):

before symmetric RFI pre-stage and contained profile and baseline cancel 45 % 21 % 15 % component at the window edge 77 % 53 % 0 % N = 2 73 % 49 % 30 % W50 / S / cz off by > 30 % / 30 % / 40 km/s 53 / 60 / 51 % 40 / 43 / 34 % 39 / 36 / 36 % the same for the 96 sources above cz = 1000 km/s 35 / 33 / 30 30 / 28 / 26

Above 1000 km/s, about a dozen sources whose fit had settled on structure at the window edge, 700–1000 km/s from the catalogue line, now find the line (e.g. AGC 748902, 222316, 7286). The 24 sources below 1000 km/s sit at or behind the Galactic cut at 350 km/s, where a line at the catalogue velocity no longer fits inside the window; the fit then describes the wing of Galactic HI with a broad component (14 detections, 13 of them flagged), and the detected fraction among them drops from 79 % to 58 %. These sources need the Galactic emission modelled, not a single-spectrum fit.

A random sample of 500 other sources is unchanged by both steps (detected 98.2 % and 98.4 %, W50 scatter 7.0 % and 7.1 %, 7.2 % before), and narrow test lines (Δv = 20–50 km/s, S/N 5–8) lose no channel to the mask. The rest of the catalogue keeps the earlier fits; refitting all of it with the new defaults changes the masks of about 15 % of the spectra, mostly by one or two channels.

docs.title: Marginal likelihood
docs.text:
For fixed \(\theta\) the model is \(m = M\beta\) with the design matrix \(M = [R, D, \dots, T_0, \dots, T_K]\). With the prior \(\beta \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \Lambda)\) and the noise covariance \(C\),

\[ \mathbf y \mid \theta \sim \mathcal N(M\mu,\; C + M\Lambda M^\top). \]

With the whitening \(L^{-1}\) (\(C = LL^\top\)) and the Woodbury identity only a \(p\times p\) system is solved, \(p\) = number of amplitudes + K + 1:

\[ A = \Lambda^{-1} + \tilde M^\top\tilde M,\quad b = \tilde M^\top \tilde r,\quad \ln L = -\tfrac12\left[\tilde r^\top\tilde r - b^\top A^{-1} b + \ln|C| + \ln|\Lambda| + \ln|A| + n\ln 2\pi\right] \]

and \(\beta\mid\theta, y \sim \mathcal N(\mu + A^{-1}b, A^{-1})\). The tests compare this with the dense formula and with a numerical integral over \(\beta\).

docs.title: Linear and nonlinear parameters
docs.text: Each profile component has five nonlinear parameters, \(\theta = (v_\mathrm{ctr}, \Delta v, \Delta v_\mathrm{rand}, \alpha, f)\), and one linear amplitude, the integrated flux \(S\). The kernel still returns the ring and disk basis functions separately; the likelihood combines them into the unit-flux column \((1-f)R + fD\). An earlier version kept \(a_\mathrm{ring} = S(1-f)\) and \(a_\mathrm{disk} = Sf\) as two linear amplitudes. That is cheaper by one sampling dimension but has two drawbacks: for narrow profiles ring and disk are nearly identical and the two amplitudes become degenerate with large anti-correlated values, and the implied prior on \(f\) (the ratio of two half-normal amplitudes) depends on \(S\), flat for faint and peaked for bright sources. With \(f\) sampled, its prior is explicit and the same for every source, and the degeneracy becomes a flat direction in \(f\) that the prior handles.

docs.title: Amplitude positivity
docs.text:
The amplitude \(S\) of each component has a half-normal prior (scale priors.amplitude_scale), i.e. a zero-mean Gaussian truncated to \(S \ge 0\). The truncation enters the likelihood exactly through the orthant probability of the conditional Gaussian,

\[ p(y \mid \theta, K) = p_\mathrm{gauss}(y \mid \theta, K)\; P(S \ge 0 \mid \theta, y, K)\, 2^{q}, \]

with the normal CDF for one component and the bivariate normal CDF (Owen's T function) for two. For three or more components the product of the marginal probabilities is used in the sampling target and the remaining correction is estimated by Monte Carlo and applied as importance weight (hiprofile.inference.amplitudes). The fraction of Gaussian draws with a negative amplitude is reported as negative_fraction; with the half-normal prior in the target it is informational.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text:
Per-channel \(\sigma\) comes from the input or a robust estimate (MAD of first differences, corrected for the channel correlation; optionally restricted to noise.signal_free ranges). The covariance between channels i and j is \(C_{ij} = \sigma_i\sigma_j\,\rho(|i-j|)\); masked channels are dropped, and the banded covariance is factorised once (banded Cholesky for NumPy, dense inverse factor for JAX). priors.noise_scale optionally fits a global scale factor.

Real spectra are smoothed in the channel domain (spectrometer window, Hanning, regridding to a velocity grid, averaging of Doppler-shifted scans), which correlates neighbouring channels. noise.correlation:

value correlation auto (default) the smoothing in model.response (hanning, kernel(...)) plus an estimated white part; white without smoothing estimate measured on the residuals of the robust pre-fit: white noise smoothed by an unknown symmetric kernel \([h_2, h_1, 1, h_1, h_2]\) with \(h \ge 0\) plus a white part, fitted to the variance ratios of the 2nd–4th to the 1st differences of the residuals; white, 3-tap and 5-tap models are chosen by AIC white, hanning, hanning-decimated, [ρ₁, ρ₂, …] fixed; a +white suffix adds an estimated white part

Two details keep the noise model safe on real data. Its power spectrum is kept above 0.5 % (+white) or 1 % (estimate) of the mean (a white floor); an exact Hanning model has zero power at the Nyquist frequency, real spectra do not, and whitening with it amplified that component by orders of magnitude (χ²_red up to 10⁴ on ALFALFA spectra). And the estimate is positive definite by construction, so masks and gaps cannot break the Cholesky factorisation. Differences rather than the sample autocorrelation, because the residuals also contain baseline ripple and line residues at low frequencies, which bias the autocorrelation (on ALFALFA spectra ρ₃ down to −0.27) and which a smoothing kernel cannot represent; differences suppress them and weight the high frequencies that the whitening divides by. Non-negative taps, because every physical smoothing has them; a free kernel turns noise in the higher lags into side lobes with deep spectral notches. The price: ρ₂ of a broad kernel is determined to about 0.03 only, which changes the noise of a flux integrated over a line by about 2 %. The fitted correlation is stored as the metrics noise_rho and noise_rho1. estimate costs one extra pre-fit iteration when the RFI pre-stage is off. Validation compares the options on noise smoothed by a kernel the fit does not know: a close guess written into model.response is as good as the true correlation, estimate is slightly overconfident (coverages 2–5 points low), ignoring the correlation is useless (85 % false positives). Use estimate only when the smoothing is unknown.

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text: Chebyshev polynomials of order K = k_min … k_max with a Gaussian prior (baseline_scale, or mean/covariance from signal-free neighbour spectra via hiprofile.likelihood.baseline.baseline_prior_from_spectra). K is compared by evidence with a flat prior.

docs.title: RFI
docs.text:
1. Pre-stage (rfi.prefit): EM fit of profile + baseline with the outlier mixture of Hogg, Bovy & Lang (2010), \(L_j = (1-P_b)\mathcal N(y_j\mid m_j,\sigma_j) + P_b B(y_j)\), with a broad background \(B\), symmetric by default (rfi.background; positive restricts it to excess flux). Output: outlier probabilities \(q_j\) (stored and plotted).
  2. Main fit: channels with \(q_j\) above rfi.threshold are masked (action: mask) or their \(\sigma\) inflated by \(1/\sqrt{1-q_j}\) (action: inflate). A single channel between two outliers is masked with them. Many outliers set the rfi flag.
  3. Extension: model.n_rfi adds narrow Gaussian components (width priors.rfi_sigma_channels, 0.3–1 channel by default) to every model.

Two guards keep the pre-stage from eating signal. Its line model is not allowed to be narrower than rfi.min_sigma_channels (2) channels, so a bright spike cannot be absorbed as a "line" and hide its own centre from the mask. And a run of outlier channels longer than rfi.max_width (20 km/s, gaps of up to two channels included, at least one channel) is not RFI but signal the one-component pre-stage cannot explain, typically a second line or a narrow dwarf, and stays in the fit; broader RFI needs a larger value or model.n_rfi. The limit protects only runs above the pre-stage model: a run below it cannot be emission and is masked whatever its length (rfi.mask_negative_runs). On ALFALFA spectra these are the dips next to strong continuum sources, which the main fit otherwise reproduced as a positive profile on a strongly negative baseline (see the ALFALFA page). The limit is in velocity so that 1 km/s and 15 km/s channels behave alike: at 15 km/s only single-channel spikes are RFI, and a line narrower than one channel cannot be told from one. hiprofile validate --stage detection measures the completeness with and without the pre-stage.

docs.title: Model comparison
docs.text:
For each spectrum the models N = 0 … n_max are evaluated; the baseline order K = k_min … k_max is marginalised inside the likelihood,

\[ p(y \mid \theta) = \sum_K P(K)\, p(y \mid \theta, K), \qquad P(K) \text{ flat}. \]

Because the Chebyshev columns are nested, \(A_K\) is the leading principal block of \(A_{K_\max}\): one Cholesky factorisation gives \(\ln|A_K|\) and \(b_K^\top A_K^{-1} b_K\) for every K as partial sums, so marginalising over K costs about as much as a single order. Consequences:

  • one sampler run per N (no K scan, no reweighting, no re-runs);
  • the posterior is exactly marginalised over K; every sample carries \(P(K \mid \theta, y)\), and the order stored with a sample (k_samples) is drawn from it;
  • the per-(N, K) evidences follow from the run without extra sampling, \(Z_{N,K} = Z_N\, \mathbb E_\mathrm{post}[P(K\mid\theta,y)] / P(K)\);
  • an informative baseline prior from neighbour spectra (mean or covariance) fixes K = k_max, because the leading-block trick needs independent zero-mean coefficient priors.

N = 0 has no nonlinear parameters and its evidence is analytic for every K. For N ≥ 1 a quick fit (MAP + Laplace + importance sampling) runs first; if its evidence lies more than sampler.gate_margin (5) nats below a model with fewer components, the sampler is skipped and the quick evidence kept (method = quick-gated). Otherwise the sampler runs once on the K-marginal likelihood (method = marginal).

A second, fainter line is a needle in the prior volume: random starts and prior-drawn particles rarely place a component on it. Two warm starts take care of that without touching the evidence. For N ≥ 2 the quick stage also optimises the N − 1 solution with a new component on each of the strongest features of the N − 1 residual (matched filters of 2 and 6 channels, sampler.n_seeds). The SMC then draws sampler.init_fraction (25 %) of its particles from the quick stage's importance proposal and the rest from the prior; the initial importance weights prior/q₀ of this defensive mixture keep ln Z exact and are bounded by 1/(1 − 0.25). Every second MCMC move of the SMC is an independence proposal from the same mixture (exact Metropolis–Hastings), so particles can jump into the narrow mode of a faint second line at every temperature instead of having to random-walk there. On pairs whose second line has S/N ≈ 6 (ln Z of N = 2 within a nat of N = 1) this brought the SMC evidence from 2–5 nats below nautilus to within a nat.

Model probabilities use a Poisson prior on N (mean poisson_rate) and the flat prior on K; the detection probability is \(P(N\ge 1\mid y)\). Several components are compared through evidences, not trans-dimensional sampling.

docs.title: Samplers
docs.text:
All backends implement run(loglike, prior_transform, ndim) -> SamplerResult (samples, weights, ln Z ± error, runtime, number of likelihood calls, statistics).

backend role smc default: adaptive tempered SMC (1000 particles, random-walk moves), one batched likelihood call per step; with --gpu (JAX likelihood) the batch runs as one XLA call nautilus most precise ln Z, fewest likelihood calls, but ~10x slower here because its neural-network training dominates for a cheap likelihood; default check_backend dynesty second opinion, well-documented diagnostics ultranest robustness check, conservative ln Z errors quick MAP + Laplace + adaptive importance sampling; quick look and start values, may miss modes

Modes: --mode quick (quick backend everywhere), --mode full (sampling of all N and K), --mode check (additionally runs check_backend at K* and flags \(|\Delta\ln Z| > 3\sigma\)).

Every nested sampler has a time / call budget (nautilus 600 s or 10⁶ calls, dynesty and UltraNest 10⁶ calls); a fit that hits it gets the sampler_budget flag.

docs.title: Accuracy and speed
docs.text:
Measured on a 512-channel spectrum (S/N 15, first-order baseline), eight seeds per setting:

backend N = 1: ln Z bias / scatter / time N = 2: ln Z bias / scatter / time nautilus (reference) – / 0.02 / 10 s – / 0.03 / 40–46 s smc, 1000 particles, 10 moves −0.04 / 0.10 / 0.9 s +0.25 / 0.23 / 3.2 s smc, 1000 particles, 20 moves 0.00 / 0.11 / 1.8 s +0.16 / 0.11 / 6.6 s quick −0.03 / 0.02 / 0.3 s −0.1 / 0.1 / 0.7 s (low ESS)

dynesty and UltraNest lie 0.05–0.15 above nautilus for N = 2, so part of the SMC offset is nautilus' own.

The SMC runs as two independent runs of 500 particles whose samples are pooled and whose evidences are averaged; the spread between the runs gives the evidence error (the incremental-weight variance of one run misses the correlation that the MCMC moves leave between particles). Measured on a single-line spectrum at S/N 8 with K = 0…3 marginalised, six seeds: the K-marginal ln Z_N of N = 1 scatters by 0.15 (reported 0.10), that of N = 2, whose second component has a broad flat posterior, by 1.0 (reported 0.3; nautilus lies within 0.3 of the SMC values). The per-(N, K) evidences of an improbable K carry an extra Monte-Carlo noise of about 1 nat from \(\mathbb E_\mathrm{post}[P(K\mid\theta,y)]\); model probabilities use the sum over K and are unaffected. Offsets of a few tenths in ln Z change model probabilities by tens of per cent at most; use --backend nautilus or --mode check where precise evidences matter.

docs.title: Compiled kernel and likelihood
docs.text:
With numba installed (a default dependency), the ring/disk kernel and the Woodbury algebra run as compiled loops (hiprofile.model.fast, hiprofile.likelihood.fast): table-based Bessel functions (Estrin scheme), recurrences for the phase factor and the Gaussian, direct scattering into the folded spectrum, banded whitening and a small Cholesky solve per parameter vector. They agree with the NumPy reference to 1e-12 (tests/test_fast.py). One evaluation of the marginal likelihood (one component, 512 channels, K = 2) takes about 19 µs in batches and 36 µs as a single call; the NumPy path takes about 100 µs and 300 µs.

Complete fits with the default configuration (N ≤ 2, K = 0…3, RFI pre-stage), one process:

spectrum before (NumPy kernel, nautilus) now (numba, smc) pure noise 15–55 s 3.4 s one component 100–220 s 4.9 s two components 100–250 s 9 s

benchmarks/bench_kernel.py and benchmarks/bench_fit.py reproduce the numbers.

docs.text: The original Cython implementation (lineprofile, emcee-based) lives in legacy/ as a frozen reference. CI builds it and checks that it still reproduces the golden files.

Tested with Python 3.12, NumPy 2.5, Cython 3.3, FFTW 3.3.10. Changes needed:

docs.title: Model, units and parameters (legacy)
docs.text:
• LineModel(velocities, n_disks, n_gaussians, n_baseline, supersample=2); parameter vector per disk (log10 S, v_sys, v_rot, v_turb, f_solid, asym) = (log10 S, v_ctr, Δv, Δv_rand, f, α), then per Gaussian (log10 S, v, log10 σ), then baseline coefficients (plain polynomial in x ∈ [-1, 1], highest order first, Horner scheme — not Chebyshev).
  • Evaluation on n_chan * supersample points with spacing dv / supersample starting at the first channel centre, periodic without padding, then the mean of each block of supersample points. Consequences: the profile is shifted by dv (s-1) / (2s) (a quarter channel for s = 2) and wraps at the band edges.
  • Fit classes FitGaussian, FitLaplacian, FitMixture (Hogg-style outlier mixture with parameters (log10 P_b, log10 σ_in, μ_out, log10 σ_out)), priors: Gamma on Δv (k = 4.38, θ = 55.4, from HIPASS), shifted Gamma on Δv_rand, Beta(1, 5) on f, Beta(10, 10) on (α+1)/2, normal on v_ctr and baseline. Note: FitGaussian.ln_bounds_likelihood tests p <= -3 and p >= 3, which is never true, so the bound is not applied.

docs.title: Golden files and benchmark
docs.text:
legacy/make_reference.py writes tests/reference/golden_profiles.npz: a full factorial grid Δv ∈ {10⁻³, 50, 230, 500}, Δv_rand ∈ {2, 8, 25}, f ∈ {0, 0.3, 1}, α ∈ {−1, −0.2, 0, 1} (random S and non-integer centres) on four grids (dv = 2, 5, 10.24 km/s; supersample 2 and 4), plus legacy log-posterior values. The new kernel reproduces all 432 profiles to 1×10⁻¹¹ relative to the peak (acceptance: 10⁻⁶).

tests/reference/benchmark_legacy.json: one legacy model evaluation takes 27 / 50 / 112 / 206 µs for 256 / 512 / 1024 / 2048 channels (supersample 2, single profile, x86_64). benchmarks/bench_kernel.py writes the comparison to tests/reference/benchmark_new.json. On the same grid as the legacy code (supersample 2, no padding) the compiled kernel computes ring and disk in 3.5 / 7.2 / 16 / 39 µs per parameter vector in batches (5–8x faster than legacy) and 13 / 17 / 21 / 59 µs as single calls (2–3.5x faster).

docs.title: Not reproduced
docs.text: The fit of a THINGS spectrum from Table 1 of the paper needs the THINGS global profiles, which are not part of this repository; hiprofile simulate with template_files accepts such profiles as templates once available.

docs.title: Line profile
docs.text:
One component is the profile of Stewart et al. (2014): a rotating outer ring (double horn) and a solid-body inner disk (half ellipse), multiplied by an asymmetry term and convolved with a Gaussian for random motions. With \(u = 2 (v - v_\mathrm{ctr}) / \Delta v\):

\[ s(v) = \left[ \frac{2 S (1-f)}{\pi \Delta v} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} + \frac{4 S f}{\pi \Delta v} \sqrt{1-u^2} \right] (1 + \alpha u) \ast \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta v_\mathrm{rand}^2) \]

The six parameters are the centre \(v_\mathrm{ctr}\), the width \(\Delta v\), the dispersion \(\Delta v_\mathrm{rand}\), the asymmetry \(\alpha \in [-1, 1]\), the integrated flux \(S\) and the solid-body fraction \(f \in [0, 1]\).

docs.title: Linear and nonlinear parameters
docs.text:
The kernel does not return a finished curve but two unit-flux basis functions, ring \(R(v;\theta)\) and disk \(D(v;\theta)\), already including asymmetry, Gaussian and channel response. With \(\theta = (v_\mathrm{ctr}, \Delta v, \Delta v_\mathrm{rand}, \alpha, f)\) the model is linear in the flux and the baseline:

\[ m(v) = S\,\big[(1-f) R(v;\theta) + f D(v;\theta)\big] + \sum_{k=0}^{K} c_k T_k(v). \]

\(S\) and the \(c_k\) are marginalised analytically, and so is the baseline order \(K\) (see Inference); the sampler sees the five nonlinear parameters per component.

docs.title: Fourier-space evaluation
docs.text:
With \(x = \Delta v\,\omega/2\):

\[ \hat R(\omega) = [J_0(x) - i\alpha J_1(x)]\,P(\omega),\qquad \hat D(\omega) = \left[\frac{2 J_1(x)}{x} - 2 i\alpha \frac{J_2(x)}{x}\right] P(\omega) \] \[ P(\omega) = e^{-i\omega v_\mathrm{ctr}}\, e^{-\Delta v_\mathrm{rand}^2\omega^2/2}\, H(\omega) \]

\(H\) is the spectrometer response (below). The inverse transform runs on a periodic fine grid (spacing \(\Delta v_\mathrm{chan}/s\)), zero-padded so that a profile inside the band never wraps around, and is sampled at the channel centres. Sampling every \(s\)-th point equals an inverse FFT of the spectrum folded modulo the coarse grid length, so the NumPy kernel only evaluates the Bessel functions where the Gaussian factor is above \(10^{-13}\) and only runs a short FFT.

J2/x and J1/x are evaluated without cancellation for \(\Delta v \to 0\). JAX has no j0/j1; hiprofile.model.bessel implements them (power series below \(x = 12.5\), Hankel expansion above, accurate to \(3\times10^{-12}\), finite gradients everywhere). NumPy uses SciPy's Cephes routines.

The default supersampling makes the truncation of the Gaussian at the fine Nyquist frequency smaller than \(10^{-7}\) for the smallest allowed \(\Delta v_\mathrm{rand}\).

docs.title: Spectrometer response
docs.text:
model.response is a +-joined list:

term \(H(\omega)\) meaning none 1 point sampling boxcar \(\mathrm{sinc}(\omega\Delta v_\mathrm{chan}/2)\) mean over the channel (default) hanning \(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12\cos(\omega\Delta v_\mathrm{chan})\) 3-tap Hanning smoothing, exact tukey(r) Tukey taper up to \(\pi/\Delta v_\mathrm{chan}\) lag window of a correlator kernel(w₀, w₁, …, w_q) $\sum_{ j

Example: boxcar+hanning. With noise.correlation: auto the channel smoothing (hanning, kernel) also sets the noise correlation, e.g. \(\rho = (1, 2/3, 1/6)\) for Hanning, plus an estimated white part.

docs.title: Sampling parametrisation
docs.text: The samplers work on the unit cube; each parameter is the inverse CDF of its prior (Priors) applied to one cube coordinate. Several profile components are ordered, \(v_{\mathrm{ctr},1} < v_{\mathrm{ctr},2} < \dots\), by mapping the unit cube to uniform order statistics, which removes label switching without changing the evidence.

docs.title: Legacy compatibility
docs.text: hiprofile.model.legacy_profile reproduces the legacy Cython LineModel (point samples on an unpadded grid averaged in blocks, which shifts the profile by \(\Delta v_\mathrm{chan}(s-1)/(2s)\) and wraps it at the band edges). It shares the Fourier coefficients with the new kernel and is only used to compare with the golden files; it agrees to \(10^{-11}\) relative to the peak.

docs.title: Priors
docs.text:
The default priors are calibrated on the fits of the 34 THINGS galaxies in Table 1 of Stewart, Blyth & de Blok (2014) and on the priors the authors used for their low-S/N fits (their Appendix B.2). They are slightly wider than THINGS because a survey contains more dwarfs, more disturbed systems and lower S/N.

parameter default THINGS fits other references Δv gamma, shape 2.3, scale 83 km/s (median 166, 16–84 % 77–305 km/s), ≤ 800 km/s; fitted to the W50 of 25 434 ALFALFA detections 0.1–566 km/s, median 153 (KS p = 0.75 against the gamma prior); two dwarfs with Δv ≈ 0 Stewart B.2: log-normal 2.2 ± 0.3, which the log-normal fit to ALFALFA reproduces (2.19 ± 0.31) Δv_rand log-normal, log₁₀ = 1.1 ± 0.2 (≈ 12.6 km/s), 4–60 km/s 8–32 km/s, median 12.4, log₁₀ 1.13 ± 0.16 Stewart B.2: 1.17 ± 0.14; resolved HI dispersions ≈ 10 ± 2 km/s (Tamburro et al. 2009); narrow / broad super-profile components 6.5 ± 1.5 / 16.8 ± 4.3 km/s (Ianjamasimanana et al. 2012) α normal(0, 0.25) truncated to [−1, 1] median 0.00, robust σ 0.14; 3 of 34 with |α| > 0.6 (NGC 3077, NGC 1569, Ho I) Stewart B.2: normal(0, 0.2) f Beta(1, 3), density 3(1 − f)², median 0.21, P(f > 0.7) = 2.7 % median 0.15, mean 0.23, 1 of 34 above 0.7 (0.93); a uniform prior is rejected (KS p < 0.001), Beta(1, 3) is not (p = 0.13) Stewart B.2: exponentially decreasing with characteristic constant 0.3 (printed as 0.3 e^(−0.3 f), which would be nearly flat; the text describes a decreasing prior) v_ctr uniform over the positions where the whole component lies inside the band minus 5 % margins (contain); normal(v_cat, 20–50 km/s) for targeted spectra – Stewart B.2: normal, σ = 20 km/s S half-normal; scale amplitude_scale: auto = max(10 × noise of the band-integrated flux, 2 × positive band flux), i.e. noise-set near the detection threshold and flat over a bright source (a narrower prior would split bright sources into pairs); fix per survey – Stewart: flat (improper, unusable for evidences) K flat over k_min … k_max, coefficients N(0, baseline_scale²), auto = 10 × rms the misspecification stage checks the K choice with a prior 50 × too wide Stewart: order by maximum evidence

All priors are simple one-parameter-family shapes (gamma, log-normal, truncated normal, beta, uniform, half-normal). The flux S keeps a half-normal prior so that it can be marginalised analytically; positivity enters the sampling target exactly through the orthant probability (see Inference). f is a sampled parameter with its own prior: an implicit f prior from two amplitude scales would depend on S.

Components inside the band. With priors.contain (default) every profile component lies entirely inside the band minus the v_margin margins: v_ctr ± (Δv/2 + 3 Δv_rand), which reaches about 1 % of the horn height. The prior is built in sequence: Δv_rand and then Δv keep their shapes and are only truncated further where no line of that width fits the band, and v_ctr is uniform over the positions where the whole component fits. A fixed window therefore does not favour narrow lines, and where the band minus its margins is wider than 1160 km/s the width priors are unchanged. Without it a component could sit half outside the window and take up a baseline slope or the wing of Galactic HI. Several components are labelled in the order of their relative position in that allowed range (not strictly of v_ctr). A posterior pressed against the limit (edge_band_<i>) raises prior_edge: the line is probably cut by the window. Containment needs a uniform v_ctr prior; an explicit range v_ctr: {low, high} stays the range of the centre.

Rotational width. W50 mixes the rotational width Δv with the random motions, the asymmetry and the solid-body fraction, so Δv cannot be read off a W50 histogram. benchmarks/fit_width_prior.py forward-models it instead: it draws profiles with Δv from a candidate prior and Δv_rand, α, f from the defaults, computes their W50 with the model and fits the candidate's parameters to the quantiles of the observed log W50. On the 25 434 HIcode 1 detections of ALFALFA α.100 (rest-frame W50, median 170 km/s, 0.29 dex, skewed towards narrow lines):

Δv prior quantile misfit KS distance previous default, log-normal 2.2 ± 0.4 dex 0.079 dex 0.106 log-normal fitted, 2.19 ± 0.31 dex 0.058 dex 0.077 log-normal × sin i (isotropic inclinations), 2.32 ± 0.27 dex 0.045 dex 0.060 gamma fitted, k = 2.3, θ = 83 km/s 0.033 dex 0.043 gamma × sin i, k = 3.3, θ = 74 km/s 0.031 dex 0.038

The gamma is skewed towards small widths in log Δv like the data and falls off exponentially above 300 km/s like the velocity function of massive galaxies; projecting it with random inclinations hardly improves the fit and is left out. The previous 0.4 dex were a setting without data and predicted far too many very wide lines. The calibration describes the detected population of a flux-limited single-dish survey out to cz ≈ 18 000 km/s; deeper or interferometric surveys (WALLABY, FAST) select differently and should run the script on their own W50 catalogue (--catalog FILE --w50-column ...). The gamma density vanishes like Δv^1.3 towards Δv = 0: face-on or dispersion-dominated dwarfs get their width through Δv_rand, which leaves W50 right but makes the split between Δv and Δv_rand a prior statement (prior_dominated).

Solid-body fraction. f is the fraction of the HI inside the radius where the rotation curve turns over. In spirals that radius is small compared with the HI disk, so most of the gas sits on the flat part and f is small; only dwarfs whose rotation curve rises across the whole disk approach f ≈ 1. A uniform prior gave such solid-body profiles 30 % of the prior mass, and at low S/N, where the data barely constrain f, it pulled posterior medians to 0.5–0.8 even for 350 km/s wide lines. Beta(1, 3) follows the THINGS distribution and keeps f > 0.7 possible (2.7 %) but rare. Physics also says that f should fall with galaxy mass, but the THINGS fits show only a weak trend with Δv (Spearman r = −0.22, p = 0.22), and Δv is V_rot sin i, so a prior on f conditional on Δv would also penalise face-on spirals; f keeps a single prior.

The simulator draws from the same priors (hiprofile simulate, all validation stages), so simulated galaxies look like the ones the fit expects.

docs.title: Survey-specific settings
docs.text:
• Single-dish surveys (HIPASS, ALFALFA, EBHIS, FAST): standing waves need higher baseline orders; Stewart et al. needed K = 6 for EBHIS. Use model.k_max: 6 and a baseline prior from signal-free neighbour spectra (hiprofile.likelihood.baseline.baseline_prior_from_spectra).
  • Interferometric surveys (WALLABY, THINGS-like cubes): K ≤ 1 is usually enough.
  • Targeted spectra with an optical redshift: priors.v_ctr: {kind: normal, mean: <v_cat>, std: 30}.
  • Evidence comparisons across a survey: set priors.amplitude_scale to a fixed value (e.g. the 95th percentile of the expected integrated fluxes).

At high S/N the data dominate and the priors hardly matter; at low S/N they regularise the degeneracy between Δv and Δv_rand. Objects outside the THINGS range (very disturbed or very narrow profiles) are pulled towards typical values; the prior_edge flag marks posteriors that pile up at a prior boundary, and prior_dominated marks fits whose Δv posterior is not much narrower than the prior (the width is then a prior statement, not a measurement). The bias study in Validation measures the pull for fixed true profiles: from S/N 8 upwards the posterior median of W50 is unbiased to within 11 km/s; at S/N 5 a 430 km/s line is pulled down by 22 km/s with these priors and by 137 km/s with flat (log-uniform) priors, so the THINGS priors are kept as defaults.

References: Stewart, Blyth & de Blok (2014), A&A 567, A61 (arXiv:1405.1838); Ianjamasimanana et al. (2012), arXiv:1207.5041; Oman (2022), arXiv:2108.08856; Tamburro et al. (2009), AJ.

docs.title: 1. Simulate test spectra
docs.text:
hiprofile simulate --config examples/simulate.yaml --n 200 --out sims --seed 1

This writes sims/spectra/*.fits, a list file sims/spectra.txt and the truth table sims/truth.csv (true N, component parameters, W50/W20, S/N, RFI channels).

docs.title: 2. Quick look
docs.text:
hiprofile fit sims/spectra.txt --mode quick --jobs 8 --out quick

quick uses MAP + Laplace + importance sampling: seconds per spectrum, good start values, but no guarantee for multimodal posteriors.

docs.title: 3. Full fit
docs.text:
hiprofile fit sims/spectra.txt --config examples/survey.yaml --jobs 8 --out results

Inputs can also be a glob ("data/*.fits") or a catalogue table with a path column (other columns are kept as meta_*), or with cube, ra, dec columns to extract aperture spectra from a cube. Column names and units are detected automatically; override them with --flux-column, --velocity-unit, --frequency-column, --convention etc. Frequency axes are converted with the radio convention by default, which keeps a uniform grid uniform.

On a cluster:

sbatch examples/slurm_array.sh      # --chunk $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID/100 --resume
hiprofile report results            # catalogue + report once all chunks are done

docs.title: 4. Inspect
docs.text:
open results/report.html
hiprofile plot results sim000042         # plots for one spectrum
hiprofile plot results --flagged         # all flagged spectra

from hiprofile.io import read_result

res = read_result("results/spectra/sim000042.h5")
post = res.posteriors[1]
print(res.p_detect, post.summary()["W50_1"])

docs.title: 5. Validate
docs.text:
hiprofile validate --stage sbc --n 1000 --jobs 32 --out validation
hiprofile validate --stage detection --stage misspec --n 500 --jobs 32 --out validation
hiprofile validate --stage injection --spectra signal_free.txt --n 500 --out validation
hiprofile validate --stage sbc --n 1000 --chunk 3/50 --out validation   # one SLURM array task
hiprofile validate --stage sbc --n 1000 --resume --out validation       # analysis once all chunks are done

Each stage writes validation/validate_<stage>/summary.md, summary.json and plots; see Validation.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Everything on this page comes from runs of benchmarks/validate_all.sh on a 4-core machine with the default configuration (full mode, SMC sampler, N ≤ 2, K ≤ 3, RFI pre-stage, Δv ~ Gamma(2.3, 83 km/s), f ~ Beta(1, 3)), 5 km/s channels unless stated otherwise. SBC, detection and misspecification were refitted at d053ea5, with profile components contained in the band (priors.contain; simulations and fits use it) and the current RFI pre-stage (symmetric outlier background, runs below the model masked whatever their length). The bias and ALFALFA fits were made at commit 2724f8a (the Δv prior), and later commits only add the Springob et al. (2005) widths, which benchmarks/add_springob.py computed from the stored spectra and baselines (the naive values are reproduced exactly), and the Hanning bias run. The low-S/N bias decomposition (benchmarks/w20_bias.py) ran at b0f5c72, the same fitting code. The correlated-noise study is from 61a2b05 with the earlier log-normal Δv prior; it tests the noise model, which the prior does not touch.

Classical references. Every stage measures the widths in two classical ways on the same baseline-subtracted spectra, in a window of ±(W20/2 + 25 % + 2 channels) around the posterior v_sys, as a by-eye window would be chosen:

  • naive: outermost channels above 50 % / 20 % of the peak channel, interpolated linearly to the next channel outward;
  • Springob et al. (2005) W_F50, as used for the ALFALFA catalogue widths: per horn, a straight line fitted to the flank between the first channels below 85 % and 15 % of (horn − rms), read at 50 %; for Hanning-smoothed spectra minus their instrumental correction 2 Δv_chan λ(S/N). Read at 20 % of the same lines it gives a W20, which is our extension of the method (λ is calibrated for W_F50 only). Where a flank cannot be fitted (fit rising away from the horn, crossing outside the window) it gives no value; that happens for 18 % of the detected SBC lines, nearly all at S/N < 8.
stage command spectra SBC hiprofile validate --stage sbc --n 1000 --seed 11 1000 detection hiprofile validate --stage detection --n 200 --seed 21 200, fitted twice misspecification hiprofile validate --stage misspec --n 100 --seed 31 5 × 100 conditional bias python benchmarks/bias_study.py --n 20 --priors default\|flat, and --response boxcar+hanning 3 × 500 low-S/N bias causes python benchmarks/w20_bias.py --n 100, and --variants default --response boxcar+hanning 1500, fitted three times; 1500 Hanning correlated noise python benchmarks/correlated_noise.py --n 300 --n-noise 150 450, fitted four times real data python benchmarks/alfalfa_study.py 10 ALFALFA sources

docs.title: Stage 1: simulation-based calibration
docs.text:
Every simulation is drawn from the fit priors: the five shape parameters, the flux (half-normal, scale 4 Jy km/s) and a Chebyshev baseline of order K ~ U{0, …, 3} with coefficients from the baseline prior; white noise with σ = 0.01 Jy on 512 channels. The fit uses the same priors with the order marginalised. The rank of the truth among 99 posterior draws must then be uniform, and the posterior intervals must cover the truth at their nominal rate.

parameter rank p-value 68 % coverage 95 % coverage v_ctr 0.07 0.71 0.96 Δv 0.80 0.68 0.94 Δv_rand 0.11 0.71 0.94 α 0.87 0.67 0.95 S 0.45 0.68 0.95 f 0.13 0.69 0.95 W50 0.03 0.68 0.96 W20 0.52 0.68 0.95

The 68 % coverages lie inside the ±2σ band for 1000 simulations (0.65–0.71), the 95 % coverages inside theirs (0.936–0.964). Seven of eight rank histograms pass (p ≥ 0.07); the W50 histogram has p = 0.03 (counts 112, 104, 79, 88, 99, 129, 92, 108, 87, 102 in ten bins), one high and one low bin without a slope or U shape. With eight tests, one p below 0.05 turns up by chance in a third of all runs; the previous run, without containment, had the same pattern in Δv_rand (p = 0.03) and a flat W50 (p = 0.10). The faint draws of the flux prior that are not detected take part like every other simulation.

Baseline order. The most probable K is the true one in 93 % of the simulations and P(K_true | y) averages 0.88; the reliability curve (right panel) follows the diagonal. The confusion matrix (rows: true K, columns: most probable K) is one-sided:

  267      1      0      0
   14    227      2      0
    5     15    219      1
    1      6     26    216

A true K = 3 whose highest coefficients happen to be small is read as K = 2, the right answer for terms the data cannot see. This calibration holds when the baseline prior matches the baselines; Stage 3 shows what happens when it does not.

Flags. 12.9 % of the fits carry a flag: prior_edge 6.8 % (Δv_rand at its 4 km/s bound for faint, narrow lines), prior_dominated 3.4 %, wiggle 2.0 %, ppp 1.0 %, multimodal 0.8 %, residual_structure 0.1 % (its calibrated false-alarm rate).

The same simulations measured against the truth (739 detected, N = 1; median error and robust scatter):

quantity Bayes naive Springob W50 [km/s] 0.0 ± 10.6 −0.3 ± 21.0 −7.4 ± 21.5 (607 measured) W20 [km/s] 0.4 ± 11.6 28.9 ± 37.0 −8.8 ± 32.5 S [Jy km/s] 0.01 ± 0.38 0.05 ± 0.39 – v_sys [km/s] −0.3 ± 4.8 −0.5 ± 8.5 −0.2 ± 9.2

The posterior medians are unbiased with half the scatter of either classical width. Each classical method fails in its own way at low S/N: noise peaks above the 20 % threshold make the naive W20 too wide, and in these unsmoothed 5 km/s channels a noise dip next to a horn ends the Springob flank search early, so its widths come out too narrow below S/N ≈ 15. Above S/N ≈ 25 all three agree (figure). The SBC population is drawn from the prior with unsmoothed channels; for Hanning-smoothed spectra, where Springob's method is at home, see the bias study below.

Example posterior (corner plot of a low-S/N spectrum with a bimodal centre):

docs.text:
200 spectra with N = 0, 1, 2 (probabilities 0.4, 0.4, 0.2), integrated S/N 2–40 per component, a first-order baseline and single-channel RFI spikes (2–3 per spectrum), fitted with and without the RFI pre-stage and the automatic flux-prior scale.

with RFI pre-stage without false positives, P(detect) > 0.5 / 0.9 0 of 77 / 0 83 % / 83 % completeness S/N 3–5 / 5–8 / ≥ 8 0.50 / 0.88 / 1.00 0.90 / 1.00 / 1.00 flagged 4.0 % 86 %

Confusion matrix with the pre-stage (rows: true N, columns: most probable N):

   77      0      0
   19     64      0
    2     17     21
  • N = 0 and N = 1 are separated cleanly: no false positive at any threshold, and no single line split into two. Without the pre-stage the RFI spikes are fitted as lines (83 % false positives, 64 % flagged unresolved, 48 % residual_structure); its higher "completeness" is the same effect.
  • The completeness at S/N 3–5 is that of the SBC, which has no RFI, so the pre-stage costs none.
  • N = 2. Of the 19 pairs with both components at S/N > 6 and separated by more than their width, 17 are fitted as N = 2. Pairs with a second component below S/N 6 (21 of 40) are mostly fitted as N = 1: a second line at S/N 3 is not detectable on its own either.
  • Widths of the detected single lines (bias ± scatter, km/s): W50 0.0 ± 9.9 (naive −1.2 ± 12.3, Springob −4.5 ± 12.8), W20 0.0 ± 9.2 (naive 25.6 ± 30.5, Springob −3.8 ± 19.6).
  • The symmetric pre-stage (current default) against the earlier positive-only one: no false positive either way; completeness at S/N 3–5 0.50 instead of 0.55 (one line of 20). Narrow test lines (Δv = 20 and 50 km/s at S/N 5 and 8, 50 each) lose no channel to the mask.

docs.title: Stage 3: misspecification
docs.text:
Five sets of 100 one-component spectra at S/N 5–80: model profiles (clean); profiles the model does not generate (template: tilted-ring galaxies with a rising rotation curve, inclinations 30–85°, lopsidedness up to 30 % and central HI holes, integrated on a fine grid); model profiles on a sinusoidal baseline that no Chebyshev polynomial up to K = 3 describes; model profiles with RFI and no pre-stage; and Chebyshev baselines of order 0–3 whose coefficients are 50 times smaller than the fit's automatic prior scale.

set flagged W50 bias / scatter [km/s] 68 % coverage of W50 W50 scatter naive / Springob W20 bias / scatter: Bayes, naive, Springob clean 8 % −0.3 / 4.9 0.71 10.6 / 10.0 0.8 / 4.4, 7.4 / 19.8, 2.9 / 9.7 template 6 % −1.5 / 6.1 0.72 11.8 / 10.6 0.6 / 6.7, 18.7 / 26.4, 0.3 / 12.7 sine baseline 100 % −1.8 / 31.6 0.28 29.5 / 24.6 −2.3 / 44.9, 2.1 / 51.0, 1.0 / 33.9 RFI unmasked 100 % −96 / 122 0.15 106 / 57 −105 / 135, −120 / 140, −29 / 61 baseline prior 50 × too wide 12 % 0.8 / 7.4 0.71 12.2 / 11.0 1.2 / 6.6, 24.1 / 36.5, 2.2 / 14.2
  • The model describes the galaxy-like templates well enough that the widths stay unbiased and calibrated, with less scatter than either classical method, which see the same profiles.
  • When the model is wrong the posteriors are overconfident, as any posterior of a wrong model is, but the flags catch it: residual_structure marks every sine-baseline fit and ppp 98 % of them (the symmetric pre-stage masks some of the wave's troughs as runs below the model, which widens the W50 scatter from 25 to 30 km/s there); ppp, prior_edge, unresolved, residual_structure (88 %) and wiggle mark the RFI fits. Unmasked RFI hurts the Springob widths least, because a spike rarely lies on a flank; it is still the flagged fits that tell the user something is wrong.
  • A wrong baseline prior leaves the line parameters unbiased and calibrated, but not the baseline order: the most probable K is right in 41 % of the spectra, nearly always too low (23 of 28 true K = 3 are fitted as K = 0). Coefficients of 0.2 σ per channel are barely visible, and with a prior 50 times too wide the Occam factor wins. The p_k columns of the catalogue are calibrated only with a fitting priors.baseline_scale, for example from signal-free neighbour spectra (hiprofile.likelihood.baseline.baseline_prior_from_spectra).

docs.title: Conditional bias: priors and classical methods
docs.text:
The SBC shows that the posteriors are calibrated on average over the prior. For a given galaxy the posterior median is still pulled towards typical values when the data are weak. The bias study fixes the true profile on a grid of widths (Δv = 20–400 km/s, Δv_rand = 12 km/s, α = 0.1, f = 0.25) and integrated S/N (3–40), simulates 20 spectra per cell and fits them with the default priors and with flat priors (log-uniform Δv and Δv_rand, uniform α and f). A third run repeats the default-prior case with Hanning-smoothed spectra (the line and white noise smoothed alike, so the integrated S/N is unchanged and the channel rms drops to 0.61 of it), fitted with model.response: boxcar+hanning; that is how ALFALFA and most single-dish spectra are delivered, and where Springob's correction applies. Medians are over the spectra the fit detects (P(detect) > 0.5).

Largest |median error| over the widths, in km/s (in brackets: median of the per-cell scatter):

channels S/N W50 Bayes W50 naive W50 Springob W20 Bayes W20 naive W20 Springob unsmoothed 5 31 (29) 36 (53) 141 (27) 29 (31) 69 (36) 153 (39) unsmoothed 8–40 10 (5) 31 (7) 136 (7) 5 (7) 103 (13) 135 (7) unsmoothed 15–40 4 (4) 12 (5) 9 (4) 2 (5) 82 (11) 10 (6) Hanning 5 19 (23) 23 (49) 167 (19) 26 (37) 94 (43) 155 (16) Hanning 8–40 5 (5) 9 (7) 6 (5) ¹ 4 (8) 63 (10) 10 (8) ¹

¹ From 20 spectra per cell; with 100 spectra the Springob widths of 400 km/s lines at S/N 8 are −89 km/s (W50) and −81 km/s (W20) off in the median (see below), so this entry holds from S/N 15 only.

  • From S/N 8 upwards the posterior median with the default priors is unbiased to within 11 km/s in W50 and 5 km/s in W20 for every width, on either kind of channel.
  • Springob et al. (2005) is as good as the fit for W50 on Hanning-smoothed spectra from S/N 15 (bias ≤ 3 km/s, the same scatter), and at S/N 8 for lines up to Δv = 100 km/s. For wider lines at S/N 8 the 20 spectra per cell of this study are too few: with 100 (next section) the Springob W50 of 400 km/s lines is 89 km/s too narrow in the median, by more than 50 km/s in 64 % of the spectra, where the fit is off by −10 km/s. On unsmoothed channels and at S/N 5 it fails for wide lines (−70 to −170 km/s). The per-channel S/N of a 400 km/s line at integrated S/N 8 is about 1, and the first noise dip below 15 % of the horn ends the flank fit inside the profile.
  • The naive threshold crossing is fine for W50 but not for W20: noise peaks above 20 % of the peak channel widen it by up to 100 km/s for wide lines, still +46 km/s at S/N 15 with Hanning smoothing.
  • At S/N 5 the default priors pull a 400 km/s line down by 31 km/s and 20–100 km/s lines up by up to 20 km/s (unsmoothed; 16 and 19 km/s with Hanning). The flat priors pull the wide line down by 137 km/s and a 200 km/s line by 42 km/s. A flat prior is therefore not the unbiased choice: the log-uniform width prior puts most of its mass at small widths, and the faint wings of a wide line are lost in the noise and the baseline whatever the prior.
  • Selection. At S/N 5 only about half of the 20 km/s lines are detected (45 %, 60 % with Hanning), and those that are are the ones whose noise made them look brighter and wider: their W20 is 23–29 km/s too wide, and the 68 % interval of W20 covers the truth in 11 % (42 % with Hanning) of them. This is a property of the detected subsample, not of the posterior: over all simulations the SBC coverages hold. The prior_dominated flag marks up to half of the fits at S/N 5 (the 400 km/s lines); the width of a line at S/N ≤ 5 is largely a statement of the prior, not a measurement.

docs.title: Where the low-S/N bias comes from
docs.text:
benchmarks/w20_bias.py refits the cells at S/N 3, 5 and 8 with 100 spectra each (unsmoothed channels unless stated otherwise, no baseline in the data) three times: with the default configuration, with only a constant baseline (K = 0), and with a Δv prior uniform on 0–800 km/s. Medians are taken over all spectra (the N = 1 posterior exists for every spectrum), over the detected and over the undetected ones, with bootstrap errors.

Δv, S/N detected all detected undetected K = 0 only, all uniform Δv prior, all 400 km/s, 3 12 % −163 ± 9 −102 ± 14 −168 ± 9 −166 ± 12 +84 ± 9 400 km/s, 5 70 % −48 ± 9 −28 ± 7 −92 ± 19 −48 ± 10 +44 ± 14 400 km/s, 8 100 % −5 ± 2 −5 ± 2 – −6 ± 2 +2 ± 2 200 km/s, 5 82 % +6 ± 3 +7 ± 4 +6 ± 6 +5 ± 3 +64 ± 12 20 km/s, 5 61 % +48 ± 9 +22 ± 5 +134 ± 23 +47 ± 8 +62 ± 27

W20 error in km/s (true W20 431 km/s for Δv = 400, 50 km/s for Δv = 20).

  • Not small numbers. With 100 spectra per cell the negative W20 bias of wide lines at S/N 5 is −48 ± 9 km/s (−28 ± 7 for the detected ones; the 20-spectrum study gave −20).
  • Not a detection effect. The detected spectra are less biased than the undetected ones: detection picks the spectra whose noise made the line brighter and broader. Selection pushes widths up for every width, which is why narrow lines are too wide and wide lines less too narrow among the detected.
  • Not the baseline. Fitting with a constant baseline only changes nothing (K > 0 is the most probable order in at most 1 % of the fits).
  • It is the prior. With a Δv prior uniform on 0–800 km/s the sign flips (+44 km/s for the 400 km/s lines at S/N 5, and narrow lines become several hundred km/s too wide at S/N 3). At low S/N the posterior median moves from the truth toward the prior's typical W20 (196 km/s for the default priors): wide lines come out narrower, narrow lines wider, and lines near Δv ≈ 200 km/s are unbiased (figure: the dash-dotted line is the limit of a fit that has learned nothing). The default prior makes 400 km/s rotation rare (P(Δv > 400 km/s) = 7 %), and with a per-channel S/N of about 1 the data cannot overrule that.

Are the intervals still right? On average over the population, yes; for one width, no. In the SBC the 68 % / 95 % coverage of W20 is 0.61 / 0.94 for true S/N < 2, 0.64 / 0.93 for 2–3 and 0.66 / 0.88 for 3–4 (143, 59 and 67 spectra; all inside their ±2σ bands). For fixed widths at S/N 3 it is 0.03 / 0.20 for Δv = 20 km/s, 0.12 / 0.81 for 50, 0.56 / 0.98 for 100, 0.92 / 0.99 for 200 and 0.41 / 0.97 for 400 km/s. The posterior there is the prior (its 16–84 % width, 240 km/s, equals the prior's), and a 20 km/s line has W20 = 50 km/s, below the prior's 2.5 % quantile of 58 km/s: the prior's own 95 % interval excludes it. In the SBC the 18 spectra with S/N < 4 and W20 < 100 km/s are all outside their 68 % intervals, those with W20 > 350 km/s 74 % of the time; the many lines in the middle of the prior make up for them. At S/N 5 the fixed-width coverages are 0.67–0.88 except for the narrowest lines (0.25). For undetected spectra the prior_dominated flag is not set, as no profile flag is (P(detect) < 0.5 already says the width is not measured); among the detected spectra at S/N 3 it marks 17–50 %.

This is the conditional bias that comes with a calibrated posterior: over the population the prior describes, the errors average out (SBC), for one kind of galaxy they do not. Uses that need widths unbiased for a fixed true width at S/N ≤ 5 (Tully–Fisher samples selected by width, for example) should cut at S/N ≈ 8, where the bias is below 6 km/s for every width, or fit the width distribution hierarchically.

docs.title: The classical methods at low S/N
docs.text:
The same 1500 spectra, and a second set with Hanning smoothing (line and noise smoothed alike, fitted with model.response: boxcar+hanning), are measured with both classical methods: once in the window the pipeline uses, around the posterior v_sys and W20, and once in a window of the same size around the true values with a constant baseline from outside it, the best case for an observer who knows where the line is.

W20 error, all spectra [km/s] Bayes naive, true window naive, fit window Springob, true window Springob, fit window 20 km/s, S/N 5, unsmoothed +48 +12 +67 −4 +9 400 km/s, S/N 5, unsmoothed −48 +102 +46 −127 −188 400 km/s, S/N 8, unsmoothed −5 +107 +91 −136 −139 20 km/s, S/N 5, Hanning +32 +8 +38 0 +7 400 km/s, S/N 5, Hanning −41 +83 +28 −138 −183 400 km/s, S/N 8, Hanning −5 +84 +76 −89 −81

Springob gives no value for 5–45 % of the spectra (flank not fittable); those are left out of its medians.

  • Neither classical method shrinks toward a prior, but both have biases of their own that do not go away with S/N for wide lines at S/N ≤ 8: the naive W20 grows with the width (+80 to +107 km/s at 400 km/s: noise peaks keep the 20 % crossing at the window edge), the Springob W20 shrinks (−90 to −140 km/s: noise dips end the flank fit early). Hanning smoothing reduces the Springob failures but does not remove them.
  • The pipeline window passes the prior on. Measured around the posterior, both classical methods inherit its pull at S/N 3: the window of a prior-dominated fit is too wide for a narrow line (naive +210 km/s instead of +15) and too narrow for a wide one.
  • Where the classical methods win is the narrowest lines at S/N ≤ 5 in a window around the truth: Springob's W20 of 20 km/s lines is unbiased where the posterior median is 30–50 km/s too wide. An observer can only place that window, however, when the line is visible, which at S/N 3 it mostly is not.

No choice of prior removes the conditional bias at low S/N, because there is no information on the width there; the default priors keep it smallest for the population they were calibrated on. What the fit adds over a good classical method is therefore not a better W50 for bright (S/N ≳ 15), smoothed lines, but the W20, the low-S/N and unsmoothed cases, calibrated uncertainties, detection probabilities, the separation of blended components and the marginalisation over the baseline.

docs.title: Correlated noise
docs.text:
The SBC simulations with the noise smoothed by a Gaussian kernel of 0.8 channels that the fit does not know (ρ₁ = 0.67, ρ₂ = 0.21, ρ₃ = 0.03, as after regridding; the line itself is not smoothed), plus 150 line-free spectra, fitted with four noise models.

noise.correlation ρ₁ used false positives P > 0.5 / 0.9 68 % coverage 95 % coverage white (correlation ignored) 0 85 % / 53 % 0.38–0.59 0.66–0.90 hanning+white (close guess) 0.65 2.0 % / 0 % 0.65–0.69 0.93–0.96 estimate 0.66 (0.63–0.70 per spectrum) 4.0 % / 0.7 % 0.63–0.67 0.90–0.94 true correlation 0.67 1.3 % / 0 % 0.66–0.71 0.94–0.97
  • Ignoring the correlation is not an option: most line-free spectra become detections and every interval is far too narrow.
  • A close guess written into model.response is as good as the truth. auto, which takes the correlation from the smoothing in the response, stays the default.
  • estimate measures ρ₁ to ±0.035 per spectrum but leaves the posteriors slightly overconfident (coverages 2–5 points low). Use it only when the smoothing is unknown.

docs.title: Channel widths
docs.text:
The runs above use 5 km/s channels. Surveys range from 1 to 15 km/s; the pipeline was checked at both ends with simulated dwarf (W50 ≈ 25 km/s) and spiral (W50 ≈ 260 km/s) profiles at S/N 10 with RFI spikes and a baseline:

channels dwarf spiral time per fit 1 km/s, 1000 channels W50 25 (22–29) for 28 mean W50 error −3 km/s over 4 seeds 13–19 s 5 km/s, 512 channels 26 (23–30) for 26 +4 km/s 8–10 s 15 km/s, 170 channels 26 (22–30) for 25, flagged unresolved 268 (258–277) for 260 5–11 s

Everything physical is in km/s (model, priors, derived widths), and the channel response integrates the profile over channels of any width. The longest run of outlier channels the RFI pre-stage may mask was once three channels; at 15 km/s that masked 25 km/s dwarfs (3 of 3 lost), so it is now rfi.max_width = 20 km/s (at least one channel). A line narrower than one channel cannot be told from a spike at that resolution; the unresolved flag (W50 below two channels) marks it. The cost of a fit scales with the number of channels times the supersampling that the narrowest allowed Δv_rand needs (7 at 15 km/s, 1 at 1 km/s).

docs.title: Real data: low-S/N ALFALFA sources
docs.text:
Ten sources from the ALFALFA α.40 catalogue (Haynes et al. 2011), drawn at random: six with HIcode 1 (S/N 6.5–9) and four with HIcode 2 (S/N 5–6.5, confirmed by an optical redshift). The spectra come from NED (baseline subtracted, Hanning smoothed, 5.2 km/s channels) and are fitted in a ±1000 km/s window with the default configuration and model.response: boxcar+hanning; widths and fluxes are converted to the cz scale of the catalogue.

W50 in km/s, S in Jy km/s; naive and Springob measured by hiprofile on the same spectra, in the window around the posterior. ¹ The classical window is centred on the first fitted component, here the bump, not the catalogue source. The systemic velocities agree within 1.7σ of the posterior errors (3–78 km/s) for all sources but the confused AGC 732650.

  • HIcode 1: all six widths and fluxes agree with the catalogue within the combined errors. In two spectra hiprofile prefers N = 2, but the catalogue source is one of the components and is measured correctly; the extra component sits on the rising edge of the extracted window or on a broad 3 mJy bump that is not in the catalogue. The automated Springob widths reproduce the catalogue's (which were measured the same way, interactively) to 4–35 km/s, about as well as the posterior medians do.
  • HIcode 2: one of four agrees. Two are confused: a catalogued neighbour 2.9′ and 3.8′ away (inside the 3.5′ Arecibo beam) overlaps in velocity, and the single-spectrum fit measures the blend, which the ALFALFA team separated with the maps; in AGC 260144 the Springob edge fit happens to pick the catalogue galaxy's flanks (135 km/s) and the posterior is broad (211–392 km/s) and flagged prior_dominated. In the third (AGC 232843, S/N 5.2) the catalogue measured the bright horn only; the posterior is bimodal between that and a 400 km/s profile with the weaker emission on the far side, and its 16–84 % range covers both.
  • Solid-body fraction: the f medians are 0.08–0.27, apart from the two blends of two galaxies (0.45, 0.52), whose summed profiles are genuinely dome-shaped.
  • Noise: the automatic Hanning + white model gives ρ₁ = 0.64–0.66. With an exact Hanning model every fit was flagged with χ²_red up to 10⁴: real smoothed spectra have a little power at the Nyquist frequency, where the exact kernel has none, and the whitening amplified it by orders of magnitude; the estimated white part (0.5–4 % here) removes that.
